title: Who, what, where, when
description: Ask where, when, how, why, how many, who, what and which.

guide.summary: Question words ask for one missing piece of information: a place, a time, a reason, a quantity, a person or a thing. Pick the word that matches the answer you expect, put it first, then choose one of the three ways French builds a question.

sections.title: Which question word?
sections.text: Think of the answer you expect. The kind of information it gives you names the word.
steps: Imagine the answer: a place, a time, a means, a reason, a number, a person, a thing?
Take the word in that row.
Put it at the front of the question, then add one of the three structures.

examples.en: How do you get to work?

watch: Comment asks the way or the means (à vélo, en train), never the reason.
Où (where) carries an accent; ou without one means “or”.

sections.title: Why, and how the answer starts
sections.text: Pourquoi asks for a reason. The reply opens with parce que, which loses its e before a vowel.
steps: Ask for a reason with pourquoi at the front.
Open the reply with both words, never with parce on its own.
Look at the word that follows: before a vowel, drop the e and write an apostrophe.

examples.fr: Pourquoi est-ce que tu restes ici ?

watch: Parce alone is not a word in French; it always travels with que.
Car joins two clauses inside one sentence; it does not open a reply on its own.

sections.title: How much, how many
sections.text: Combien asks for a quantity or a price. Before a noun it always takes de, whatever the gender or the number of that noun.
steps: Is a noun coming next? If not, combien goes straight to the verb.
With a noun, put de between them: never des, never les.
Before a vowel or a silent h, de becomes d’.

examples.fr: Combien de cafés bois-tu par jour ?
examples.en: How many coffees do you drink a day?

watch: Never combien des pommes: the link stays de even in the plural.
Combien d’amis, but combien de livres: the apostrophe only appears before a vowel sound.

sections.title: Three ways to build the question
sections.text: After the question word, French offers three structures. All three are correct: plain order is spoken, est-ce que is the safe written choice, inversion is the most formal.
steps: Put the question word first.
Choose one structure and one only.
After est-ce que, the subject stays in front of the verb.
With inversion, join the verb and the pronoun with a hyphen: vas-tu, partez-vous.

examples.fr: Comment est-ce que tu vas à l’école ?
examples.en: How do you get to school?

watch: Où est-ce que travailles-tu ? marks the question twice: keep one structure.
In casual speech the question word slides to the end: Tu vas où ? Tu fais quoi ? That is fine when talking, but write the question word first.

sections.title: Asking about a person
sections.text: Qui asks about a person, whatever job that person has in the sentence.

rows: qui + verb, or qui est-ce qui + verb
Qui vient ? / Qui est-ce qui vient ?
qui + est-ce que, or qui + inversion
Qui est-ce que tu vois ? / Qui vois-tu ?

steps: Check that the missing information is a person.
Decide whether that person does the action or receives it.
As subject, the verb follows straight away, in the singular; as object, add est-ce que with normal order, or invert the verb and the pronoun.
watch: As subject, qui takes a singular verb: Qui vient ?, not Qui viennent ?
Qui never elides: qui est, never qu’est.

sections.title: Asking about a thing
sections.text: For a thing as object, the opening depends on the word order you use after it.

rows: at the end, in speech only

steps: Decide the order: subject first, or verb first?
Subject first takes the long opening; inversion takes the one-word opening.
Elide before a vowel: qu’est-ce qu’il, qu’est-ce qu’elle.
Never use the long opening and inversion together.

examples.fr: Qu’est-ce que tu fais ce soir ?

watch: Que tu fais ? is wrong: the one-word opening needs inversion behind it.
Qu’est-ce que veux-tu ? marks the question twice; after that opening the subject comes first.
In writing, a question never starts with quoi.

sections.title: After a preposition: qui or quoi?
sections.text: When the verb needs a preposition (parler à, penser à, parler de, avoir besoin de), that preposition opens the question. A person is then qui, a thing is quoi.
steps: Find the preposition the verb or the answer uses.
Put it at the very front, before the question word.
A person is qui, a thing is quoi; que can never follow a preposition.

examples.en: Who are you going on holiday with?

watch: English ends with the preposition (who with?); French never does.
Avec que and de que do not exist.
Pourquoi in one word asks for a reason; pour quoi in two words asks for a purpose.

sections.title: Which one? The forms of quel
sections.text: Quel asks which one out of several. It belongs to a noun and agrees with it, even when est stands in between.
steps: Find the noun the question is about.
Check its gender and its number.
Take the matching form; all four sound the same, so only the spelling shows the agreement.
watch: Quel âge as-tu ? — French asks “which age do you have”.
In Quelle est ta couleur préférée ?, the agreement reaches across est to couleur.
Quel always comes with a noun; with no noun, another question word is needed.

steps: Read the answer and name what it gives: a place, a time or a means.
Pick the question word from that row of the table.
Put it first, then keep one of the three structures.
Asking for a cause: open the question with pourquoi.
Answering a cause: open the reply with both words, never with parce alone.
Check the next word: before a vowel the e drops and an apostrophe takes its place.
Ask about a quantity or a price with combien.
If a noun follows, put de between them, never des or les.
Elide de to d’ before a vowel or a silent h.
Check that the missing information is a person.
Decide whether that person does the action or receives it.
Subject: the verb follows directly and stays singular. Object: use est-ce que with normal order, or inversion.
Find the preposition the verb or the answer uses (à, de, avec, pour).
Move it to the very front, in front of the question word.
A person after a preposition is qui; que is impossible there.
Check that you are asking about a thing, not a person.
Look at what follows: subject first, or verb first?
Subject first takes the long opening, elided before a vowel; inversion takes the one-word opening.
Never combine the long opening with inversion.
Check that the thing you ask about comes after a preposition.
Put that preposition at the very front of the question.
After a preposition, a thing is quoi, never que.
Find the noun the form belongs to, even when est separates them.
Decide that noun’s gender and number.
Write the form of the table that matches both.
Keep the question word at the front.
Choose exactly one structure: plain order, est-ce que, or inversion.
After est-ce que the subject stays before the verb; with inversion, hyphenate the verb and the pronoun.

exercises.instruction: Choose the question word that fits the answer.
exercises.source: — ____ tu vas ce week-end ? — À la mer.
exercises.hint: The answer names a place.
exercises.feedback: Match the question word to the kind of information in the answer.
exercises.explanation: À la mer is a place, so the question word is où, where.

mistakes.why: Quand asks about a time, so the reply would name a day or an hour. À la mer names a spot on the map.
Comment asks in what way or by what means, and would be answered à vélo or en train. À la mer is not a means of travel.

exercises.instruction: Choose the question word that fits the answer.
exercises.source: — ____ est-ce que le film commence ? — Demain soir.
exercises.hint: The answer names a time.
exercises.feedback: Match the question word to the kind of information in the answer.
exercises.explanation: Demain soir is a time, so the question word is quand, when.

mistakes.why: Où asks about a place, so the reply would be a cinema or a town. Demain soir names a moment instead.
Comment asks in what way something happens. Demain soir tells you the moment the film starts, not the manner.

exercises.instruction: Write the question word that fits the answer.
exercises.hint: The answer describes a way of doing something.
exercises.feedback: The reply is about the means of travel, not a place or a time.
exercises.explanation: À vélo says how, so the question word is comment.

mistakes.why: Où asks about a place, and the reply would be au bureau. À vélo names the means of transport, not the destination.
Quand asks about a time, answered by a day or an hour. À vélo says nothing about the moment.
Pourquoi asks for a reason and is answered with parce que. À vélo gives no reason.
Combien asks for a quantity or a price, answered by a number. À vélo is neither.

exercises.instruction: Translate into French.
exercises.source: When are you leaving? (to a friend)

alternatives.message: That works in casual speech, with the question word at the end. In writing, put the question word first.

exercises.hint: Use partir for tu, with the question word first.
exercises.feedback: Start with the word for when, then use one of the three question structures.
exercises.explanation: Quand goes first, followed by normal order, est-ce que, or inversion: Quand pars-tu ?

mistakes.why: This mixes two structures: est-ce que already marks the question, so the subject must stay in front of the verb after it.
Est-ce on its own is not the marker; the small linking word after it is missing before the subject.
Vous is the polite or plural form. The task says to a friend, so partir needs its tu form.

exercises.instruction: The answer is: À Lyon. Fix the question word.
exercises.hint: À Lyon answers a question about a place.
exercises.feedback: The structure is fine. Only the question word does not match the answer.
exercises.explanation: A place is asked with où: Où habites-tu ?

mistakes.why: This is the sentence unchanged: it still asks about a moment, while the reply À Lyon names a town.
Changing the structure does not help: the sentence still asks about a moment, and only the question word had to be swapped.
Comment would ask in what way someone lives — alone, well, cheaply. À Lyon is a place.

exercises.instruction: Choose the question word that fits the answer.
exercises.source: — ____ tu restes à la maison ? — Parce que je suis malade.
exercises.hint: The answer gives a reason.
exercises.feedback: An answer starting with parce que tells you which question was asked.
exercises.explanation: Parce que gives a reason, so the question asks why: pourquoi.

mistakes.why: Comment asks in what way, and the reply would be à pied or en voiture. Parce que je suis malade gives a cause instead.
Combien asks about a quantity or a price, answered by a number. The reply here explains a cause.

exercises.instruction: Complete the answer with the French for because.
exercises.source: — Pourquoi tu ne manges pas ? — ____ je n’ai pas faim.
exercises.hint: The answer to pourquoi usually begins with two words.
exercises.feedback: Write the two-word expression that gives a reason. The next word begins with a consonant.
exercises.explanation: Pourquoi is answered with parce que: Parce que je n’ai pas faim.

mistakes.why: Parce never stands alone in French: it is always followed by the small linking word that introduces the clause.
The shortened spelling is only used before a vowel sound. The next word, je, begins with a consonant, so nothing is dropped.
Pourquoi is the question word, not the reply. Repeating it gives no reason.
Car links two clauses inside one sentence (Je ne mange pas, car…). It does not open a standalone reply.

exercises.instruction: Complete the answer with the French for because, shortened if needed.
exercises.source: — Pourquoi est-ce qu’il court ? — ____ il est en retard.
exercises.hint: The next word, il, begins with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: Write the two-word expression and check what happens to que before a vowel.
exercises.explanation: Que elides before il, so parce que becomes parce qu’: Parce qu’il est en retard.

mistakes.why: Que keeps its e only in front of a consonant. The next word, il, starts with a vowel, so the e has to go.
The e is rightly dropped, but a dropped letter has to be marked with an apostrophe.
Parce alone is not French: the reason clause needs the linking word after it.
Pourquoi asks the question. The reply has to give the cause, not repeat the question word.

exercises.instruction: Translate into French.
exercises.source: Why are you laughing? (to a friend)

alternatives.message: That works in casual speech, with the question word at the end. In writing, put the question word first.

exercises.hint: The verb is rire. Put the question word first.
exercises.feedback: Start with the word for why, then use one of the three question structures.
exercises.explanation: Pourquoi comes first: Pourquoi tu ris ?, Pourquoi est-ce que tu ris ? or Pourquoi ris-tu ?

mistakes.why: Est-ce que already turns the sentence into a question, so the subject stays before the verb; inverting on top of it is one marker too many.
Parce que answers a why-question, it does not ask one: this says “because you laugh”.
Vous is for a group or for politeness. The task says to a friend, so rire needs its tu form.

exercises.instruction: Fix the reply to the question Pourquoi tu pars ?
exercises.hint: The French for because has two words.
exercises.feedback: One small word is missing from the start of the reply.
exercises.explanation: Because is parce que, never parce alone: Parce que je suis fatigué.

mistakes.why: Nothing changed: the reply still opens with a word that cannot stand on its own in French.
The shortened spelling belongs before a vowel only, and je begins with a consonant.
Car links clauses inside one sentence, so it does not open a reply here; the task was to add the missing word, not to swap it.
That turns the reply into a question about yourself instead of giving the cause.

exercises.instruction: Choose the word that follows combien before a noun.
exercises.source: Combien ____ sœurs est-ce que tu as ?
exercises.hint: After combien, a noun is introduced by the same small word whatever its gender or number.
exercises.feedback: The word after combien never changes for plural nouns.
exercises.explanation: Combien de is fixed: combien de sœurs, combien de frères. Des and les are wrong here.

mistakes.why: Des means “some” and cannot follow a quantity word. The link after combien never changes for a plural noun.
Les is the definite article (“the sisters”) and points at a known group. A quantity question points at no particular sisters.

exercises.instruction: Write the question word that fits the answer.
exercises.hint: The answer is a price.
exercises.feedback: Ask about a quantity or an amount of money.
exercises.explanation: A price answers combien: Combien coûte ce pull ?

mistakes.why: Comment asks in what way, so the reply would be en carte or en espèces. Quarante euros is an amount.
Quel needs a noun right behind it (quel prix), and it asks which one, not what amount.
Quoi never opens a written question, and it asks what, not what amount.
Pourquoi asks for a reason and would be answered with parce que. A price is not a reason.

exercises.instruction: Build the question.
exercises.source: How many coffees do you drink a day? (to a friend)
answers: Combien de cafés bois-tu par jour ?
exercises.hint: Start with combien, then the small word, then the noun.
exercises.feedback: One tile is wrong after combien.
exercises.explanation: Combien de cafés is the quantity, followed by the inverted verb: Combien de cafés bois-tu par jour ?

answers: Combien des cafés bois-tu par jour ?
mistakes.why: Des cannot follow a quantity word: that tile is the trap. The link to the noun never changes for a plural.
The noun cannot come straight after the quantity word; a small linking tile has to sit between them.

exercises.instruction: Translate into French.
exercises.source: How many children do you have? (to a friend)
answers: Combien d’enfants est-ce que tu as ?

alternatives.message: That works in casual speech, with the question word at the end. In writing, put the question word first.

exercises.hint: Combien de becomes combien d’ before a vowel.
exercises.feedback: Put combien d’enfants first, then one of the three question structures.
exercises.explanation: Combien d’enfants starts the question; de elides before enfants: Combien d’enfants as-tu ?

mistakes.why: De cannot stay whole in front of a vowel, and enfants begins with one: the e drops and an apostrophe replaces it.
Des would mean “how many of the children”, pointing at a known group. A plain quantity question never takes des.
Est-ce que and inversion are two different structures; using both marks the question twice.
A noun cannot follow the quantity word directly; the linking word is missing, elided before the vowel.

exercises.instruction: Fix the error.
exercises.hint: The word after combien does not change for a plural noun.
exercises.feedback: Look at the small word between combien and pommes.
exercises.explanation: Combien is always followed by de: Combien de pommes veux-tu ?

mistakes.why: Unchanged: des is still sitting between the quantity word and the noun, where it cannot go.
Les points at particular apples (“the apples”). A quantity question takes the fixed little link, not an article.
Removing des is only half the repair: a linking word still has to join the quantity to the noun.
The e is only dropped before a vowel sound, and pommes begins with a consonant.

exercises.instruction: Choose the question word.
exercises.hint: The answer is a person.
exercises.feedback: You are asking which person does the action.
exercises.explanation: Qui asks about a person and can be the subject of the verb: Qui veut du gâteau ?

mistakes.why: Que asks about a thing and never acts as the subject of the verb. The reply Moi names a person.
Quoi asks about a thing, and it only appears after a preposition or at the end of a spoken question, never in front of the verb.

exercises.instruction: Write the question word. The answer will be a person.
exercises.source: ____ est-ce que tu invites à ta fête ?
exercises.hint: You are asking about people, not things.
exercises.feedback: Que and quoi ask about things. Which word asks about a person?
exercises.explanation: Qui asks about a person, also when that person is the object: Qui est-ce que tu invites ?

mistakes.why: Que asks about a thing, and in front of est-ce que it is written qu’est-ce que. You invite people, not things.
That opening asks what, and it would double the est-ce que already written in the sentence.
Quoi asks about a thing and cannot open a question with est-ce que.
Quel needs a noun right behind it and asks which one out of a set, not which person.

exercises.instruction: Translate into French.
exercises.hint: The question word is the subject, so the verb follows it directly.
exercises.feedback: Start with the word for who and use the il form of the verb.
exercises.explanation: Qui as subject takes a singular verb: Qui habite ici ?

mistakes.why: Est-ce que opens an object question and needs a subject after it. Here the missing person is the one doing the living.
As a subject, the question word counts as one person for the verb, so a plural ending does not agree with it.
Que asks about a thing and can never be the subject. The question is about a person.

exercises.instruction: Ask who does the action: replace Marc with a question word.
answers: Qui est-ce qui cuisine ce soir ?
exercises.hint: Marc is a person and the subject of the verb.
exercises.feedback: Put the question word for a person in Marc’s place and keep the rest.
exercises.explanation: Qui replaces the subject Marc, and the verb stays singular: Qui cuisine ce soir ?

mistakes.why: This only adds a question mark: Marc is still named, so it asks whether he cooks rather than which person does.
The subject question word keeps a singular verb, so the plural ending does not agree with it.

answers: Qui est-ce que cuisine ce soir ?
mistakes.why: Est-ce que belongs to object questions and needs a subject behind it; here the missing person is the one cooking.
Que asks about a thing. Marc is a person, so the replacement must be the person word.

exercises.instruction: Build the question.
exercises.hint: Start with the word that asks about a person.
exercises.feedback: One tile asks about a thing, not a person.
exercises.explanation: Qui is the subject here, so it is followed directly by the verb: Qui a mangé mon gâteau ?

mistakes.why: Que asks about a thing and can never be the subject of the verb. That tile is the distractor.
The past participle cannot come before its helper verb; the helper follows the subject directly.

exercises.instruction: Choose the words that fit the answer.
exercises.source: — ____ tu vas au cinéma ? — Avec Julie.
exercises.hint: The answer names a person after avec.
exercises.feedback: Keep the preposition from the answer and choose the word for a person.
exercises.explanation: Julie is a person, so the question is avec qui. Avec quoi asks about a thing.

mistakes.why: Que can never follow a preposition: it only opens a question on its own, with inversion behind it.
Quoi does follow a preposition, but it asks about a thing — a tool, an object. Julie is a person.

exercises.instruction: Write the two words that fit the answer.
exercises.source: — ____ est ce cadeau ? — Pour ma mère.
exercises.hint: The answer starts with a preposition and names a person.
exercises.feedback: Use the same preposition as the answer, then the question word for a person.
exercises.explanation: Pour ma mère answers pour qui: Pour qui est ce cadeau ?

mistakes.why: Written in two words it asks about a thing or a purpose. Ma mère is a person.
In one word it asks for a reason, and the reply would start with parce que. This reply names the person who gets the present.
Dropping the preposition loses the “for”: the reply keeps pour, so the question must keep it too.
Que cannot follow a preposition. After pour, a person is asked about with a different word.

exercises.instruction: Translate into French.
exercises.source: Who are you talking to? (to a friend)
answers: À qui est-ce que tu parles ?

alternatives.message: That works in casual speech, with the question word at the end. In writing, put the question word first.
That is correct French for who are you talking with. Here practise parler à, which gives à qui: À qui parles-tu ?

alternatives.answer: Avec qui est-ce que tu parles ?
alternatives.message: That is correct French for who are you talking with. Here practise parler à, which gives à qui: À qui parles-tu ?
That is correct French for who are you talking with. Here practise parler à, which gives à qui: À qui parles-tu ?

exercises.hint: The verb is parler à. In French the preposition goes before the question word.
exercises.feedback: French never leaves the preposition at the end. Start with it.
exercises.explanation: Parler à gives à qui, placed at the start: À qui parles-tu ?

mistakes.why: Parler needs its preposition in front of the person; without it the sentence says “who you speak”, which is not French.
French never leaves a preposition stranded at the end of a question: it travels to the very front.
Est-ce que and inversion are two ways of asking. Using both marks the question twice.
Quoi asks about a thing, so this would mean talking to an object. The question is about a person.

exercises.instruction: Ask a question about the person after avec. Use inversion.

alternatives.answer: Avec qui est-ce que tu travailles ?
alternatives.message: That is correct, but this exercise asks for inversion.
That is correct in speech, but this exercise asks for inversion.

exercises.hint: Replace Sophie with a question word but keep avec in front of it.
exercises.feedback: Put avec and the question word first, then invert the verb and tu.
exercises.explanation: Avec qui moves to the front together, then inversion: Avec qui travailles-tu ?

mistakes.why: The preposition cannot be left at the end in French; it moves to the front together with the question word.
Quoi asks about a thing, so this asks what tool you work with. Sophie is a person.
Leaving the question word at the end is fine in speech, but this exercise asks for the inverted order.
Inversion joins the verb and the pronoun with a hyphen; without it the pair is not read as inverted.

exercises.instruction: Fix the question. The verb is parler à.
exercises.hint: Parler needs a preposition before the person.
exercises.feedback: A word is missing at the very start of the question.
exercises.explanation: The preposition of parler à goes before qui: À qui tu parles ?

mistakes.why: Unchanged: parler still has no preposition in front of the person it points to.
French never ends a question with a stranded preposition; it belongs at the very start.
That asks who you are talking with. The task repairs parler à, whose own preposition is a different one.
The missing word is added, but the rest of the sentence was fine and did not need inverting.

exercises.instruction: Choose the right question word.
exercises.hint: The verb is already inverted with tu.
exercises.feedback: One option is only used with normal word order after it.
exercises.explanation: Que is used with inversion: Que fais-tu ? Qu’est-ce que needs normal order, and quoi cannot start this question.

mistakes.why: That longer opening is followed by normal order, subject then verb. Here the verb already stands in front of tu.
Quoi only appears after a preposition or at the end of a spoken question; it cannot open a written one.

exercises.instruction: Choose the right question word.
exercises.hint: Here tu comes before the verb, in normal order.
exercises.feedback: Que alone needs inversion after it. Which option allows normal order?
exercises.explanation: Qu’est-ce que is followed by normal order: Qu’est-ce que tu fais ? Que tu fais is wrong, and qui asks about a person.

mistakes.why: On its own it has to be followed by the inverted verb, verb then pronoun. Here tu comes first, in normal order.
Qui asks about a person. Ce soir shows that the question is about an activity, a thing.

exercises.instruction: Rewrite the question with qu’est-ce que and normal word order.
exercises.hint: After qu’est-ce que, put tu back before the verb.
exercises.feedback: Change the opening and undo the inversion.
exercises.explanation: Qu’est-ce que takes normal order: Qu’est-ce que tu manges ?

mistakes.why: Nothing was changed: the sentence still uses the one-word opening with inversion.
The opening is right, but the inversion was kept; after that opening the subject goes back in front of the verb.
The opening is incomplete: est-ce needs its linking word before the subject.
That asks which person you are eating. The original question is about a thing.

exercises.instruction: Rewrite the question with que and inversion.
exercises.hint: Que alone needs the verb before the pronoun.
exercises.feedback: Shorten the opening to one word and invert vous and the verb.
exercises.explanation: Que is followed by inversion: Que cherchez-vous ?

mistakes.why: Unchanged: the long opening is still there, and the task was to shorten it and invert.
The opening is shortened, but the short form needs the verb in front of the pronoun, and vous still comes first.
Inversion needs a hyphen joining the verb and the pronoun.
Quoi cannot open a written question; it lives after a preposition or at the end of a spoken one.

exercises.instruction: Fix the question.
exercises.hint: Qu’est-ce que and inversion do not go together.
exercises.feedback: Either keep qu’est-ce que with normal order, or keep the inversion with que alone.
exercises.explanation: Qu’est-ce que already marks the question, so tu stays before veux. Que veux-tu ? is the inverted version.

mistakes.why: Unchanged: the long opening and the inversion are still fighting over the same job.
The subject is now written twice. After that opening, one subject in front of the verb is enough.
Quoi cannot open a written question; it belongs after a preposition or at the end of a spoken one.
Half the opening was removed: est-ce still needs its linking word before the subject.

exercises.instruction: Translate into French.
exercises.source: What are you reading? (to a friend)
answers: Qu’est-ce que tu es en train de lire ?

alternatives.message: That is common in casual speech. In writing use Qu’est-ce que tu lis ? or Que lis-tu ?

exercises.hint: The verb is lire. Use qu’est-ce que with normal order, or que with inversion.
exercises.feedback: What as the object is que or qu’est-ce que. Check the word order that each one needs.
exercises.explanation: Qu’est-ce que tu lis ? and Que lis-tu ? are both correct. Que tu lis is not.

mistakes.why: The one-word opening must be followed by the inverted verb; with the subject in front, the longer opening is the one to use.
Quoi never opens a written question. It is used after a preposition, or at the very end in speech.
The long opening already marks the question, so inverting on top of it marks it twice.
The opening is incomplete: est-ce needs its linking word before the subject.

exercises.instruction: Complete qu’est-ce que. Write only the missing part, including any apostrophe.
exercises.hint: The next word, il, begins with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: The last part of the opening elides before a vowel.
exercises.explanation: Before il, que becomes qu’: Qu’est-ce qu’il regarde ?

mistakes.why: Before a vowel the e drops, and the next word, il, begins with one, so the full spelling cannot stay.
The e is rightly dropped, but the missing letter has to be marked with an apostrophe.
After est-ce, qui opens a subject question and cannot be followed by another subject like il.

exercises.instruction: Choose the word that fits the answer.
exercises.hint: The answer is a thing, and the question word comes after a preposition.
exercises.feedback: After de, one word asks about a thing.
exercises.explanation: After a preposition, a thing is asked with quoi: De quoi as-tu besoin ?

mistakes.why: Que never follows a preposition; it only opens a question directly, with inversion behind it.
Quel has to come with a noun (de quel stylo) and asks which one out of several, not what.

exercises.instruction: Write the question word. The answer is a thing.
exercises.source: — Avec ____ tu écris ? — Avec un crayon.
exercises.hint: The answer is a thing, and the question word comes right after a preposition.
exercises.feedback: The answer is an object, and the question word follows avec.
exercises.explanation: Avec quoi asks about a thing: Avec quoi tu écris ? Avec qui would ask about a person.

mistakes.why: Que cannot stand after a preposition; it is only used at the start of a question, with the verb inverted.
After a preposition, qui asks about a person. Un crayon is an object.
Quel must be followed by a noun and asks which one, not what.

exercises.instruction: Translate into French.
exercises.source: What are you thinking about? (to a friend)
answers: À quoi est-ce que tu penses ?

alternatives.message: That works in casual speech, with the question word at the end. In writing, put the question word first.

exercises.hint: The verb is penser à, and the preposition goes before the question word.
exercises.feedback: Start with the preposition, then the word for a thing after a preposition.
exercises.explanation: Penser à gives à quoi, placed first: À quoi penses-tu ?

mistakes.why: Without a preposition this asks for an opinion, “what do you think”. Penser à needs its preposition in front of the question word.
Que can never follow a preposition, whichever preposition it is.
After the preposition, qui asks about a person: this means “who are you thinking of”.
The preposition of penser à is missing, and this word never opens a written question on its own.

exercises.instruction: Fix the question word.
exercises.source: Avec que tu coupes le pain ?
answers: Avec quoi tu coupes le pain ?
exercises.hint: After a preposition, the word for what changes.
exercises.feedback: The structure is fine. Look at the word after avec.
exercises.explanation: Que cannot follow a preposition; it becomes quoi: Avec quoi tu coupes le pain ?

answers: Avec que tu coupes le pain ?
mistakes.why: Unchanged: que is still standing after the preposition, where it can never go.

answers: Avec qui tu coupes le pain ?
mistakes.why: Qui asks about a person, so this asks who you cut the bread with. The question is about the tool.

answers: Avec qu’est-ce que tu coupes le pain ?
mistakes.why: That opening cannot follow a preposition: it is a sentence opener on its own.
Dropping avec loses the “with”, and this word still cannot stand in front of a subject.

exercises.instruction: Build the question.
exercises.hint: The verb is parler de, and the preposition goes first.
exercises.feedback: One tile cannot follow a preposition.
exercises.explanation: Parler de gives de quoi at the start: De quoi parlez-vous ?

mistakes.why: Que can never follow a preposition: that tile is the distractor here.
The preposition of parler de has been left out, and this word cannot open a question without one.

exercises.instruction: Choose the right form of quel.
exercises.hint: Quel agrees with the noun after it. Is heure masculine or feminine?
exercises.feedback: Check the gender and number of heure.
exercises.explanation: Heure is feminine singular, so quel becomes quelle: Quelle heure est-il ?

mistakes.why: That is the masculine form, but heure is feminine (une heure), so the spelling has to change.
That form is masculine and plural. Heure here is one single feminine noun.

exercises.instruction: Choose the right form of quel.
exercises.hint: Films is plural. Is film masculine or feminine?
exercises.feedback: Match both the gender and the number of films.
exercises.explanation: Films is masculine plural, so the form is quels.

mistakes.why: That is the feminine plural, but film is a masculine noun (un film).
That form is singular, while films carries an s and names several of them.

exercises.instruction: Write quel in the right form.
exercises.hint: Quel agrees with the noun it asks about, here couleur.
exercises.feedback: Couleur is feminine singular.
exercises.explanation: Quel agrees with couleur, even with est in between: Quelle est ta couleur préférée ?

mistakes.why: The masculine spelling does not fit: couleur is feminine (une couleur), even with est standing in between.
That form is masculine and plural, while one feminine noun is being asked about.
That form is plural. Couleur here is one single colour.

exercises.instruction: Write quel in the right form.
exercises.hint: Chaussures is plural. Is chaussure masculine or feminine?
exercises.feedback: Match the gender and the number of chaussures.
exercises.explanation: Chaussures is feminine plural, so the form is quelles.

mistakes.why: That is the masculine singular form, and the noun behind it is feminine and plural.
The gender is right, but chaussures ends in s: several of them are meant.
That is the masculine plural, and chaussure is feminine (une chaussure).

exercises.instruction: Fix the agreement.
exercises.hint: Langue is feminine, and here it is plural.
exercises.feedback: The form of quel does not match the noun after it.
exercises.explanation: Langues is feminine plural, so quel becomes quelles.

mistakes.why: Unchanged: the form still ignores both the feminine gender and the plural s of langues.
The gender is repaired but the number is not: langues names several.
The number is repaired but the gender is not: langue is feminine (une langue).
Making the noun singular changes the question instead of repairing the agreement, and langue is feminine anyway.

exercises.instruction: Translate into French.
exercises.source: Which bus are you taking? (to a friend)
answers: Quel bus est-ce que tu prends ?

alternatives.message: That works in casual speech, with the question word at the end. In writing, put the question word first.

exercises.hint: Which + noun is quel, agreeing with the noun. Bus is masculine.
exercises.feedback: Put quel and the noun first, then one of the three question structures.
exercises.explanation: Quel bus goes first; bus is masculine singular: Quel bus prends-tu ?

mistakes.why: Bus is a masculine noun (un bus), so a feminine spelling does not agree with it.
The plural form asks about several buses at once; only one bus is being taken here.
Est-ce que and inversion are two different structures, and only one may mark the question.

exercises.instruction: Build the question.
exercises.source: How old are you? (to a friend)
exercises.hint: French asks “which age do you have”. Âge is masculine.
exercises.feedback: Two tiles are forms of quel. Choose the one that agrees with âge.
exercises.explanation: Âge is masculine, so the form is quel: Quel âge as-tu ?

mistakes.why: Âge is masculine (un âge), so the feminine tile does not agree with it. That tile is the distractor.

exercises.instruction: Rewrite the question with est-ce que.
exercises.hint: Est-ce que goes after the question word, then normal order.
exercises.feedback: Keep où first, add est-ce que, and put tu back before the verb.
exercises.explanation: Question word, est-ce que, then subject and verb: Où est-ce que tu vas ?

mistakes.why: Unchanged: the sentence still uses inversion and no marker was added.
The marker is added but the inversion was kept; after the marker the subject goes back in front of the verb.
The marker is incomplete: est-ce needs its linking word before the subject.
The question word slid to the end. That happens in speech, but in writing it opens the sentence.

exercises.instruction: Rewrite the question with inversion.
exercises.hint: Drop est-ce que and put the verb before the pronoun.
exercises.feedback: Keep quand first, remove est-ce que, and invert vous partez.
exercises.explanation: Question word, then the inverted verb and pronoun: Quand partez-vous ?

mistakes.why: Unchanged: the marker is still there and nothing was inverted.
Inversion was added but the marker was not removed; one of the two has to go.
Removing the marker leaves plain spoken order. The task asks for the verb and the pronoun to swap places.
The two words are in the right order, but an inverted pair is joined by a hyphen.

exercises.instruction: Build the question with est-ce que.
exercises.source: How do you get to school? (to a friend)
answers: Comment est-ce que tu vas à l’école ?

alternatives.message: That is correct spoken French, but this exercise asks you to use est-ce que.

exercises.hint: Question word first, then est-ce que, then subject and verb.
exercises.feedback: Est-ce que goes between the question word and the subject.
exercises.explanation: Comment, then est-ce que, then normal order: Comment est-ce que tu vas à l’école ?

answers: Comment est-ce que vas tu à l’école ?
mistakes.why: After the marker, the subject comes before the verb; here the two are the wrong way round.
The marker tile was dropped and the verb put first. The task asks for the marker between the question word and the subject.

answers: Est-ce que tu vas comment à l’école ?
mistakes.why: The question word was left inside the sentence. In writing it opens the question.

exercises.instruction: Fix the word order.
exercises.hint: Est-ce que and inversion are two different structures. Use only one.
exercises.feedback: After est-ce que, the subject goes before the verb.
exercises.explanation: Est-ce que takes normal order: Où est-ce que tu travailles ? Without est-ce que, inversion is fine: Où travailles-tu ?

mistakes.why: Unchanged: the marker and the inversion are both still there.
The subject is now written twice. After the marker, one subject in front of the verb is enough.
The inversion is undone, but the marker lost a word: est-ce cannot stand without it.
The question word slid to the end. That happens in speech, but in writing it opens the sentence.
